title: Three disjoint directed shortest paths
formal: Does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decide whether a directed graph with positive rational arc lengths and three prescribed source-target pairs contains three mutually vertex-disjoint paths, each individually shortest between its own endpoints?

why: Three pairs form a small and sharply defined test of whether directed shortest-path constraints can be coordinated efficiently. A resolution would distinguish the difficulty of selecting individually optimal routes from ordinary shortest-path computation and from undirected routing.
status_note: The 2023 source and January 2026 follow-up both state the directed three-pair question as open. Those statements and the positive-weight model were checked on 13 September 2026. No later resolution was verified; status is source_open.

progress.text: The paper states the directed three-disjoint-shortest-paths problem as open and uses strictly positive edge weights throughout.
The later paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms and repeats the directed three-pair question as Open Problem 6.3.

category_assignment.reason: The saved question asks for polynomial-time directed three-pair disjoint shortest paths; congestion here concerns path overlap rather than a distributed communication model.

importance.reason: The first unresolved fixed number of directed disjoint shortest-path pairs, isolating a basic barrier in exact multi-pair routing.

sentences: The input specifies three source-target pairs in a directed graph with positive arc lengths.
Each selected path must be shortest for its own pair in the original graph, and no vertex may belong to two paths.
The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the full binary input length.
A 2026 paper improves randomized two-pair algorithms but explicitly leaves three pairs unresolved.
A resolution would explain whether several individually optimal directed routes can be selected efficiently while avoiding all conflicts.

definitions: The input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), with \(V=[n]\), no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair, together with a length \(\ell(a)\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) for each arc and three pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in V^2\), \(i=1,2,3\). Graph incidences and all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicitly encoded in binary. A directed path follows the arcs and has no repeated vertex; a zero-arc path is permitted when its endpoints coincide. Its length is the sum of its arc lengths. The distance \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum path length, or infinity when no path exists. A valid answer YES means there are paths \(P_i\) from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\), each of length \(d_G(s_i,t_i)\), with \(V(P_i)\cap V(P_j)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Disjointness includes all terminals. Repeated terminals across different pairs therefore force NO. Distances are measured in the original graph, not after deleting other paths; minimizing the total length of three disjoint paths is a different condition. Time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine bit time polynomial in the total encoding length, including lengths. No acyclicity or planarity promise, uniqueness of shortest paths, randomness, advice or oracle is allowed. Strict positivity follows the source preliminaries; allowing zero-length directed cycles is not part of this card.

context_blocks.text: The source’s congested shortest-path task includes mutually vertex-disjoint shortest paths as the congestion-one case. It states that the directed three-pair problem remains open even though fixed numbers of pairs are tractable on undirected graphs and directed acyclic graphs.

A January 2026 paper improves randomized algorithms for two disjoint shortest paths in general directed graphs. Its Open Problem 6.3 again asks for polynomial-time solvability or hardness of the three-pair case. The two-pair theorem and the three-pair question must remain separate.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the deterministic polynomial-time decision statement or its negation for the specified positive-rational-length model. An NP-hardness reduction is a conditional negative result under P ≠ NP and must be stated with that hypothesis. A randomized algorithm alone, an algorithm for two pairs or acyclic inputs, or a solution minimizing only total path length does not settle the exact statement.

notes: Recovered positive edge weights and vertex disjointness including terminals; corrected the old generic distributed-model context.
Specified binary rational lengths and deterministic bit time; did not silently extend to zero-length cycles or replace individual shortestness by minimum total length.
Added the January 2026 two-pair improvement and its explicit repeated three-pair open question, with the randomized scope correctly labeled.
